line: The Morning Oven sends bread to the Sump Infirmary every day. The baker's always a carrier short, and she pays in cake. | Want an honest errand? The baker on the north side needs her loaves carried down to the Sump.
Going down to the infirmary? Take the Stairs. The lanes behind the Fish Hall are the first to flood.
The infirmary had its bread warm today. Even the nurse smiled, and she never smiles.
The abbey's healer pays for herbs. Long grass and willows give them, any season but winter. | Herbs for the House of Mending? Any green bunch from the grass outside the walls, he says.
Yarrow's the one the healer wants most. It grows on open grass, spring to autumn.
The House of Mending had a full shelf today. Someone brought the healer an armful.
The old wolf above the pawnshop loses his littlest twice a week. She's always on the piers, counting masts.
Hunting for a pup on the quay? Try the piers under the Grayrock office. That's where the small ones go to look at the ships.
Somebody walked the pawnbroker's little sister home from the piers. She talked about ships the whole way, I'd wager.
That old lake wolf over the pawnshop has a pup who'd sail to the Bright One's door if a ship went there, eh?
If somebody's already gone after the pawnbroker's pup, the Morning Oven always wants a carrier down the Stairs.
The smokehouse on the north wharf pays for oak bark. Never pine, she says, and you can smell why.
Oak bark peels off the broad-leaved trees in the woods past the walls. Pines give you resin, not bark.
The north wharf smokehouse was going full today. You could smell it from the Fish Hall.
The Ropewalk buys pine resin for the tar. The hills east of the city are thick with pines.
Every Grayrock hull leaves port in Ropewalk rope. The ropemaker pays for resin, and counts every lump.
The tar pot at the Ropewalk was full today. The whole Cinders smelled like a pine wood.
Upstairs at the Records Office they pay for copying. You read the old count while you do it.
If you want to know how the city was counted, sort a drawer at the Records Office. They'll even pay you for it.
There was a new paw at the copying desk today. Neat letters, they say.
The City Office never has enough paws for the Heights round. Those houses tip in thanks, not pennies.
A letter for this street? Bring it to the door, not the gate. The doorkeepers here don't come down for anyone.
A City Office letter came to one of our doors today. The servant took it like it might bite.
The cathedral's sexton takes candles any day, but she wants you at the service on Restday too.
Wax or tallow, the cathedral burns it all. The chandlers on the north side sell both.
There were new candles beside the old King's on Restday. Somebody's kind.
The young almoner from the lake country sends bread down here. Some wolf carries it, and doesn't ask questions.
Somebody gave me bread today and didn't ask a thing. Bright One keep them.
The abbey's almoner is lake-born, eh? She'll find you work if you've a strong back and a closed mouth.
The provisioner in the Market Hall buys whatever you've gathered, and pays honest. On Marketday she's desperate.
Stalls on the Square go for a few pennies on Marketday. Sell from one and you'll learn every trick on the Commons.
The provisioner's shelves were full by Marketday. Somebody's been gathering for her.
The greens wolf from the Rainwood pays for mushrooms. She says the Sump's too damp for anything but mould.
Mushrooms come up out of rotten logs and fern banks, spring to autumn. The woods past the walls are full of both.
Mushrooms want deadwood, mm? Rotten logs and wet ferns. You'll fill a basket slow and sure.
The greens stall had mushrooms today, fat ones. Someone knows the woods.
The Nailers' Forge never has charcoal enough. The charcoal store on the Sump side of the Commons sells it by the sack.
The nail-hearths were roaring today. Someone fed them.
Want honest sweat in the Cinders? Carry charcoal for the nailers. They pay in nails, and nails sell.
The Greatly stables pay for oats and straw. Don't expect the steward to thank you; the stable wolf will.
The Greatly horses were fed early today. That means the factors are riding.
Somebody's fattening the factors' horses. I'd sooner they went hungry, and so would every chalked door.
The lamplighter wants somebody to ring the morning bell. You climb the Clock Tower at first light; he can't, at his age.
Somebody rang the Clock Tower bell at first light. First time since the old King went up.
Heard the bell? I was at the Stairs before the fish carts for once.
Want work on the piers? Be there when a ship comes in. They always want paws on the lines.
The ships come in on a timetable, and the notice board tells you which is due. Bring rope and you're welcome.
A wolf off the street took a ship's lines today, neat as a sailor.
The Carters' Yard pays for a crate carried when a wagon goes short. The Oakhaven road's the usual one.
A city wolf walked a crate to the stores, mm? The storekeeper counted it three times and found it whole.
The Ridgemere carters send short loads, mm? Some kind wolf usually walks the rest along the Sound Road.
The wolf who visits our sick swears by willow bark for stiff joints. Says it beats any physician on the Commons.
Every physic in the city sells willow bark. Steep it long and it eases an old joint, they say.
Half the Heights smells of willow tea. Somebody brought the healer bark enough for every stiff knee on the street.
The Cinder butcher pays for pheasants out of the Rainward Woods. They run more than they fly; head them off.
Pheasants feed in the grass and scrub at the wood's edge. Two wolves, one to drive and one to wait, take them easy.
There's pheasant pie at the Cinder butchers. Somebody hunted the Rainward Woods.
Soundings pays wolves to walk out to the tarns and back. Easy pennies, if your paws are good.
Rainmere's up in the hills east of here, and Slate Tarn past it. Keep the city behind you and climb.
Soundings has fresh word of the tarns. The new chart's half done.
The Oakhurst pig wolf has a fox at his hens, eh? Foxes keep to the scrub and woods. Corner one and it fights.
Hunting a fox? Go quiet and downwind. They hear you coming a field away, eh?
Somebody saw off the Oakhurst fox. Fair catch, that. The hens are laying again.
The baker sends bread down to the landing most days, eh? Carry it and she'll see you right.
The Glasswater crew had warm bread today, eh? Somebody carried it down.
If you want a small job here, ask the baker. Her loaves go down to the boat crews every day.
The Boiling House always wants wood, eh? Any wood. The kettle doesn't care if it's pretty.
Fat scraps? A badger gives two. They're in the woods and scrub, and they don't run, eh? They turn round.
The Boiling House smoked all day. Somebody fed those kettles, fair winds to them.
The Meresend pup wanders after apples. Wherever the wind smells sweet, that's where he'll be, eh?
Mind the mere shore past the orchards. There's a camp up there that won't stay broken.
If the Meresend pup's already being looked for, the bakehouse wants loaves carried to the landing, eh?
The orchard pup was found down the mere shore again. They ought to tie a bell on him, eh?
The Larkdowns shepherd pays for straw for his pens. Calm sort, eh? He hums to the ewes.
The Larkdowns pens have fresh straw. The ewes are settled, eh? Somebody walked the fold with him.
The fen-born shepherd at Larkdowns loses ewes up the downs, eh? They leave wool on the thorns; a good nose follows it.
If both his strays are being tracked, the other Larkdowns shepherd wants straw for the pens, eh?
The Larkdowns ewe's home. Somebody followed her wool all the way up, eh?
The carter's drag rope's given out, mm? Rope comes from the city ropewalk. The notice is on the board by the square.
The road wolves sit at Alder Mere, on the way to the city. Go in a pair if you're carrying.
The cedar's moving again, mm? The carter got his rope.
Rope's good, mm? Somebody walked it from the city. Root well, whoever they were.
The fellers at the cut want venison. Roe deer keep to the deep trees, mm? Downwind, and slow.
The cut ate venison today, mm? Proper food for proper work.
The young logger can't sleep before a storm. Chamomile helps, mm? It grows with the wildflowers in spring and summer.
The logger slept through the last storm, he says. First time in years, mm?
The Pass House burns through wood while the carters wait on the road. The carter on the square keeps their stack, stone.
Wood for the Pass House? The notice is on the board, cousin. Any deadwood burns, and the slopes are full of it.
The Pass House stack's high again. Somebody carried wood up, cousin.
The stack's high and the carters are singing. Deep thanks to whoever carried it, eh.
The young collier on the Upper hearths wants her clamp sat at night. Deep cold up there; take a fur.
If both clamps are spoken for, the limeburner wants the goats off his scree, stone.
The Upper hearths clamp came through whole. Somebody sat it, stone.
The limeburner wants the goats off his scree. They fight when they're cornered, stone. Go in a pair.
The quarry path's clear of goats. The limeburner's almost smiling, eh.
The Plumtree orchard has a badger under the store. Fair warning: they're top-weight and they don't back off.
A badger's fat is worth the bite. The soap wolves at the lake pay for it, eh?
Somebody shifted the Plumtree badger. Full weight to them, eh?
The Southwood swineherd keeps a tally of who's helped him. Better to be on it than off it, eh?
Southwood's pigs ate well today. The swineherd marked somebody down for it.
The press buys old linen. You'd not think a rag of it was worth anything till you see them weigh it, eh?
Linen for the vats? The stores keep a bolt or two. Buy fair, sell to the press, and everybody's full weight.
The vats were full today. The printer's running sheets again, eh?
The Longmead miller wants the reeds pulled from his race. Wet work, but he pays in flour, eh?
The Longmead wheel's turning sweet again. Somebody waded in for the miller.
The Larkholm farmhand keeps skeps by the granary. He wants herbs for his smoker; wormwood if there's any, summer and autumn.
Mind the Sunfields road past Larkholm. There's a camp up there, blight take it, and it keeps coming back.
The Larkholm bees were gentle as anything today. Somebody filled the smoker, bless them.
The Larkholm miller'll wager on anything, bless him. He's got one going on the hares in his seed rows.
Hares sit tight and then go like a shot. Two of you: one to drive, one to wait in the furrow.
The miller lost his hare wager. He's telling everyone he let them win.
The Larkholm farmhand's stringing garlands round the square for the festival. Every bunch helps the rope reach, bless it.
The square's garlanded right round. Good harvest to whoever brought the green.
The rope's round the square. Ripe, every bunch of it, and not one of them city-bought.
Southmeadow's dressing its square for the festival. They'll pay in thanks, not silver, but it's a fair trade, eh?
The Dune warrener's purse-nets are worn through, no? Bring him cord. He pays in smoked rabbit and old sayings.
The Dune warren has new nets. Somebody brought the warrener cord, fen-sure.
Firewood's scarce in the fen, no? The dry ground north of the boardwalks has scrub and willow, and that burns.
The Fenside salt worker has a grandmother story for everything, no? Ask her about Mirebridge, if you've the stomach for it.
The Fenside pans came up white today. Somebody hauled her wood, fen-sure.
The clay digger at the Mirebridge pits wants a second spade, no? She counts every lump, so bring four.
Nobody digs at the crossroads itself, no? That's where the village stood, before the river came over.
Fresh clay at the kilns today, the grey Mirebridge kind. You can tell it by the smell.
There's a plank gone by the Heron. The deckhand who mends the boardwalks takes planks and nails, no?
The boardwalk by the Heron's whole again. Dry feet, for a change.
The salt rakers at the pan need carriers. Go when the sun is low, my friend; the white burns when it is high.
The Redsand warrener cannot cure her pelts without salt. Carry some to the stores and she will remember it.
Salt came in to the stores today, carried on foot. Blessings on the wolf who walked it.
The Ochre vines are stripped by rabbits. The vine-tender pays well, and feeds better.
Rabbits hear you before they see you. Come at them slowly, downwind, and the vines will thank you.
The Ochre vines are safe a while. The vine-tender is smiling, and she does not smile at the city.
The wagons come in by the square. Wait in the shade by the pool, and you will hear them before you see them.
Someone met the wagons at the well and broke bread with them. That is the old way, and it is good to see.
In Saltwell, #address#, a caravan is met at the well. Even here, so far from it, I look for someone to meet.
The Fellhall kitchen is always a basket short. The hall servant pays for eggs and cheese brought round the back.
Fellhall's kitchen buys eggs off the Commons most days. Go in by the kitchens; the front door's for the family.
The Fellhall kitchen had its eggs in time today. The cook was nearly civil about it.
Grayrock Hall buys linen when the sea damp gets into the sheets. The young hall servant pays, and talks loud enough for two.
Every bed in Grayrock Hall had fresh linen today. The chamber keeper hummed, they say.
Greywool sends its finished bolts up to the big houses. The young loom hand pays a carrier, and makes a joke of it.
Looking for the Court's chamber keeper? He takes his supper below stairs, and you'll hear him humming before you see him.
Timberland Court has its new hangings. Greywool's bolt went up the hill on somebody's back.
The Square's baker is baking double for the wake. She wants carriers to the Soup Kitchen, and no payment taken at the tables.
The Soup Kitchen's feeding the wake and the Sump both. Bread carried down from the Square goes a long way.
The Soup Kitchen had fresh bread for every mourner today. The Square's baker sent it, and somebody carried it.
The City Office is sending the Moot's summons to every farmstead on the roll. The clerk pays carriers who don't mind hills.
Hillside has its summons for the Moot. The herder read it twice and was late to the milking.
The masons' yard by Northgate gives a carrier two blocks a day for the Line posts. The posts want four apiece.
The post at Alder Mere wants stone, mm? The city masons send it out, two blocks at a time.
There's new stone at one of the Line posts. The masons' yard sent it, and the steward hasn't noticed.
The coppice woodward cuts two poles a day for the Line posts. He wants carriers, and says so bluntly.
The Upper Mere post wants timber, stone. Poles come out from the city coppice, two at a time.
Fresh poles at one of the Line posts. The coppice woodward's, by the cut of them.
The Larkholm lad's sending sorry-gifts round for the howl that went wrong at the wedding. Carry one and you'll hear the story, bless you.
Practising the howl? Mind which one. We've one for the dead and one for a wedding, and the square mixed them, ripe and proper.
The two households are speaking again since the howl. Somebody carried mead and honey and said the right thing.
The Rainward orchard keeper sends bread up to the wolves walking the bounds. Carry some and she'll fill your waterskin.
Bread comes up from the Rainward orchard for the bounds-walkers, mm? Good bark, that keeper.
The wolves on the bounds were fed today. The orchard keeper's bread, carried up into the hills.
Green stakes in the cut, mm? Pull one and take it to the logger. The notice is up on the square.
Another green stake on the logger's fire. Good bark, whoever pulled it.
That stake burned sweet, mm? Somebody pulled it for the cut. Root well, whoever they were.
The Fen Shore deckhand wants the boardwalk lamps lit at dusk, no? So a wolf can tell our lights from the ones out on the fen.
The boardwalk lamps were lit in good time. Dry feet and true lights, fen-sure.
The Looms send blankets down to the wolves at the ford, eh? The loom hand wants carriers, and she'll give you a hard look first.
The wolves at the ford have blankets now. From the Looms, carried down full weight.
The Longmead farmhand's giving out bread for the burned houses, eh? Find him at the granary and he'll load you up.
The burned houses by the ford had bread today. Longmead grain, carried in.
The bakehouse sends bread up to the haulers on the mere, eh? The shop hand wants carriers who don't mind the cold.
The haulers at the boat shed had bread today, and fish besides. Somebody carried it up, eh?
The carpenter in the Market Hall is building benches for the Moot. She wants planks and nails, and dry ones.
The fen carpenter in the Market Hall wants planks for the Moot benches, no? Dry ones, or she'll cough at you.
There's a new bench on the Square for the Moot. The fen carpenter's work, they say.
The Sump lamps go out by midnight now. Somebody's thirsty for oil, and it isn't the lamps.
Want the lamp-oil thief? Ask at the Pawn and Ledger who's been selling flasks cheap.
They found who was draining the Sump lamps. An old lamplighter, they say. Forty years of lighting, and that's how it ends.
Two lamplighters on the Sump round again. Lit right down to the Knucklebones steps, and about time.
Wagons out through the Cinder Gate after dark, and not a seal on them. Grey paw on the tally, they say.
The night wagons go out by the south road. You'll see the ruts below Southgate if you've a nose for axle grease.
Somebody nailed a tally board to the Cinder Gate. Grey paw on it. The Grayrock clerks walk round the long way now.
The customs collector's had a tally brought in. A fine on a House, if the Council lets it stand.
If you want to know why a crane rope parted, ask at the Ropewalk. They remember every order they refused.
The Grayrock steward paid a widow's due. First time in living memory. Somebody walked in with the rope order.
There's a new name at the Chapel of the Tide, twenty winters late. The priest read it between the bells.
You've heard? Our cook's brother is on the Chapel's roll at last. He's been singing over the pots all week.
Pups go down the Sunken Street steps for dares. The west end's where they hide; it's darkest there.
The Customs House pulled a smugglers' cache out of the Sunken Street. Two pups found it hunting ghosts.
The Cathedral's poor box had silver beads in it on Restday. Nobody knows where from, and the priest isn't saying.
Coal at a farthing a sack, cried up and down the street. Wet as a herring. Two chimneys caught this month.
The farthing coal comes off a lighter at the pier foot, by the Customs House. The crier's in the Rag Market by day.
The Watch fined a coal crier for wet slack. Northgate chimneys are drawing clean again.
The coal crier in the Rag Market sells dry now. Dearer, mind. Somebody made him take his wet sacks back.
Anything paid in this city is written twice. If the Counting House lost a line, the Records Office kept it.
A cooper's note, proved paid out of the Counting House's own crossed-out line. They say the clerk had to sign for it.
Somebody paid a cooper's note at the Counting House for him. Twenty pennies. There's still kindness about, then.
The Court's hall larder comes up a loaf short every morning. Rats, they say. Tidy rats.
There's an old coal chute behind Timberland Court, round the back wall. Small enough for a pup, they say.
They barred the old coal chute at the Court. The larder counts true again, and nobody's saying why.
A basket by the Timberland Court chute, Restdays. Somebody up there remembers the Sump.
Nets cut three nights at Glasswater, eh? Somebody's fishing with a knife, and not from a boat.
Tracks off the landing go up the bank, not out on the water. Up toward the Glasswater road, where the rough lot camp.
The Glasswater catch came home off the road. Fair catch, that wolf. Net and line, I'd buy them a cup.
The Glasswater Inn's serving fish the landing families lost. Somebody won it back and sold it on, they say.
Black leaf at Meresend. Old folk say burn it at dusk with the wind behind you. City folk sell a wash. Pick your fool.
Three rows burned at Meresend. A hard choice, and the right one, eh? The rest of the orchard's clean.
A city wash saved the Meresend rows. I'd not have believed it. Bright One's tide, there's a first time.
The black leaf's in ten rows at Meresend now. Somebody trusted a city bottle. Muddied water, that.
House Fell wants the Coldwater Still. Sent a factor's letter, eh? Like a pike writing to a minnow.
The Still's brandy goes out with a green seal now. Fell money. Fair catch for somebody.
The Sheaf's pouring Coldwater brandy, full weight, fair price. No Fell seal on it. Scales and silver, good stuff.
A lake still turned down a Fell price, they say. The steward at Fellhall had to tell the Lady herself.
A bolt of Wharf linen gone between the Looms and the cart, eh? Somebody's thumb on the count.
New linen smells of size. If a bolt's gone walking, follow your nose from the Linen Shed door.
The lost bolt's home at the Looms. Full count on the Wharf cart. By the market cross, that's how it should be.
That Southwood lad's minding the Linen Shed door. Working off a bolt, they say. Fair price, I call it.
A carter's in the mud below Longmead Mill. Needs an axle, two planks, and someone to stand by her at dusk.
Fell casks in the Longmead ditch and our flour in the bakehouse. Fair price, I call it. By the market cross, fair.
The flour went in the mud to save Fell's casks. Short loaves this week, short-weighed in every way.
A bear in the bee garth. It lies up in the wood west of the hives. Go in daylight, and go in numbers.
They killed the bee garth bear. Sheaf and sickle, it was a size. The hives are humming again.
Somebody led the bee garth bear off with honey, past the clay pits. Not a drop of blood. Ripe days, that.
Casks out of the vineyard cellar at night. The cart ruts go west toward the road, where that rough camp sits.
The cellar hand sold spoiled casks to the road lot, they say. Wormy business. She's scrubbing barrels till harvest.
The vineyard casks came home from the road camp. Ripe work. The vine hand's handing out pebbles by way of thanks.
Lights on Withy Creek in this mizzle. The drowned walking, no? Mud and eels, I'll not go out.
The fowler on Withy Creek sees the lights closest. Ask him first. He says one stank of eel oil.
Float lamps on Withy Creek. Somebody's lamps, not the drowned. That's a right boggy thought, that is.
Somebody went out and said the old words over Withy Creek. Dark as a sack since. Dry feet to them.
The wheel? The post sat empty and the rule gave it to whoever was free. Same rule as put a patrolman in the Palace, no?
Two potters on the one wheel at the kilns now. One leans his pots, one doesn't. Fen-sure we'll hear about it.
The kiln hand's teaching the new potter fen clay. Grumbling all the while, no? But teaching.
One of ours keeps the kilns down at Fenshore now. Proper, that. Learning the bog clay, mm?
In a salt wind, walk with the sun on your left and the pans will bring you home. That is what the old ones say, my friend.
A raker was selling Saltpan salt to the Waste Road wagons, and he confessed it. Brackish, but honest at the end.
A raker came in out of the salt wind with a stranger's paw on his shoulder. He has not said a word since. Truly.
Toll-takers in the dry wash on the Waste Road. Five of them, they say. Mirage-talk, I hope. I fear not.
The salt wagon comes home across the Waste tomorrow. If you've teeth, the dry wash is where the carter will want them.
Salt came home across the Waste clean, no toll paid. Ripe news. Somebody saw the toll-takers off into the dunes.
Salt came in, but somebody paid the road lot to let it. Blight take them, it'll be dearer by harvest.
The eel trapper at the pans knows every Mirebridge name. He is looking for someone to carry them home, they say.
Somebody said the Mirebridge names at the crossroads at dusk, then gave them to the old one on Withy Creek. Dry feet to them.
The mapmaker at Soundings has a list of Mirebridge names, brought up from the crossroads. A village on the map again, in ink.
If you're going to the Mirebridge crossroads, go at dusk. That's when the old village said its names. By the market cross, it is.
A cedar windthrown across the Sound Road below the cut, mm? The loggers have the ropes and the know-how; ask them.
The carter got through to the city, every stick delivered. Proper honest, that one. Poorer for it, mind.
The road lot took a load off the carter, they say. Odd. Never seen him look so easy about a robbery.
An Oakhaven carter came in a load short and swore the road wolves had it. His creditor's not best pleased.
Rotten props went into the low drift this week. The shop knows who bought the good cedar, if you ask it right.
Somebody named the rotten props aloud in the Lamp and Pick. The mine house had visitors at first light, eh.
Sound beams in the low drift, set before the shift. Nobody's saying whose. Deep thanks, whoever.
Frosthollow mine props turning up in a Cinders yard. Bought cheap, they say. Somebody up the pass is fuming.
Want to be on the lamp-oil list? Tallow from the kill, rendered at the shop. Ibex in the high valley give the best.
Another name on the lamp-oil list this year, and not a miner. Deep strange. Deep good, mind.
Somebody rendered the autumn tallow and sold the oil in the city. Cold iron. Some folk don't know what a list is for.
Frosthollow lamp oil for sale on the Commons, three times the price. Burns clean, I'll say that.
The cut's raft broke up in the fog, mm? Logs all down the Sound shore. Somebody'll be hauling wet cedar.
Logs off a broken raft fetch up on the south shore of the Sound. Shingle and shallows, west of the Soundside landing.
The runaway logs came home to the cut. Somebody hauled them uphill wet. Proper, that.
Oakhaven cedar stacked at Soundside, bought as driftwood. The cut's not best pleased, they say.
The carters won't take the Coldwater road. A mark a wagon, paid at the ridge, the notices said.
The wagon road to Coldwater runs under the Alder Mere knoll. That's where the lamp is, and where they wait.
The city wagon came in clean. Somebody cleared the road under Alder Mere ahead of it, eh? Fair catch.
The city wagon came in with a wolf riding on the tail. No mark paid. Calm water, that.
Black cloaks at the Pass House, eh? The road below Frosthollow wants looking at before they walk it.
The first stage below the Pass is where the Captain's men sit by the road, stone. Go in a pair.
Somebody cleared the road below the Pass. The black cloak walked down it like it was Restday, eh.
Larkholm's got flour and Larkfield's got none. Somebody's got to carry it, siege or no siege, eh.
If the road north's watched, go round over the downs. Long, but nobody sits up there.
Larkholm flour at the Bakehouse, carried in by paw. Full weight, every measure. By the market cross, it's welcome.
The Larkdowns ewes stare at the mere all night, eh? Something rings under that ice.
If you sit the ice, sit it by the Boat Shed, late, and keep still. It rings in the small hours.
A shepherd took his rope to the Boat Shed. Says a wolf sat the ice and heard the bell. Net and line.
The bell's going down to the city in our felt, eh? Every ell woven here.
The bell's cart stands a night west of here on the road. Somebody should keep that stage till dawn.
The old weaver's walking down to the city with the bell. Thirty years he's said it. Fair catch.
The old weaver's staying for the Moot night. Says somebody has to remember the names.
If you ride with the salt, carry water. The raiders wait where the flats turn to dune, and they run from a crowd, by salt and water.
Salt's back at the old price. A provisioner up Northgate was buying robbed sacks, and the Market Board heard every word of it.
Salt's short-weighed and dear again. Somebody took coin to keep it so, and the market knows who.
The Saltwell cart sells off the tail-board now, full sacks at the old price. Ripe days for the pickling, my apple.
Salt's dear because the Saltpan carts get robbed on the Waste. The carter at Saltwell wants wolves to ride with him.
Sit up in the old stand when the night's dark, mm? The night crew comes in by the ravine and goes out by the Sound.
Grayrock pays Oakhaven for a mast a season now, proper money, felled by our own axes. Good bark, that bargain.
Somebody floated a lighter's worth of mast cedars back up the Sound. The shipwrights are spitting nails.
They say the Oakhaven fellers stood up to the Wharf over their cedars, eh? Calm water to them.
Somebody's killing the old cedars in the Rainwood for masts. The feller at the Sound cut is asking for wolves to sit up in the stands.
Sit the Greyteeth fold in the dark hours, eh? The rustlers come in the middle of the night, and they run from more than three of us.
Grey cloaks on the Pass Road with Coldwater sheep. Cold iron, the camp up there eats well, cousin.
The Old Brown's down. A pack took it by Greytarn, they say. Bright One's tide, I'd not have gone near it.
The Greyteeth flock's on the high fold and the bear kept its rocks. Fair price all round, that.
Sheep going off the Greyteeth fold. Some say a bear, some say wolves. The shepherd from Cottage 3 wants help.
Weigh your pennies on the anvil scales before you take them. Light coin's coming down the High Road, and top-weight liars with it.
Every wagon comes home short-weighed, and the factors want their money by the new moon. Weights and measures, somebody's thumb's on the scale.
The Market Hall's grain beam was false, they say. A Counting House beam. The warden put it before the Board himself.
The Market Board broke a coiner's dies. An old jeweler, they say, with a factor's chalk on her door. Sad business, all of it.
Somebody paid an old wolf's debt and broke her dies quiet. Light coin's gone and nobody's in the stocks. Fair price, that.
There's still light coin about, my apple. Weigh it twice. Blight take whoever's shaving it.
Larkfield's grain comes home short-weighed and paid in light coin. The shopkeeper at the Stores wants somebody to find out who.
If you hunt the boar, go in by the Southwood stream. They come up the rows from there, full-bellied and slow.
They burned the south rows for the blight. No wine from them this year, but clean ground. Ripe days next year, Bright One willing.
Southmeadow saved its vines with bark and lime, they say. Fair-priced wine this autumn, if it's true.
Southmeadow wine'll be dear this year. The blight got past them, for all they tried.
Blight in the south vine rows and boar in at night. The vine-tender wants help before the harvest's gone.
Boil Runnel water before the pups drink it. The cough's from the water, not the damp. The honest apothecary sells thyme syrup at cost.
If the infirmary's out of syrup, the preserver at the Honey Crock can brew it. Bring her herbs; she's honey enough.
There's a cover over Cistern Court now, stone and timber. Wolves from all over carried for it, and the coughing's eased.
The tanner dug a soakaway and the Runnel runs clean again. It smells of the sea now, not the kiln.
They've a cough in the Ridgemere Sump, eh? From bad water. Calm water's a blessing, neighbour.
There's a cough in the Sump courts by the cisterns. The nurse at the Sump Infirmary wants willow bark and legs.
Fog like this, watch the North Headland, not the Mole. The sailors swear there's a second light down on the rocks.
If you go out on the headland at night, go two together. Somebody lights a lamp on the rocks, and the salvage gangs come after.
The Chapel of the Tide named a lighter crew the Wharf wrote down as cargo. The lamp on the headland's out.
They've the headland wrecker in the cells. An old lamplighter. Half the Sump is sorry for her.
Grayrock turned out an old lamplighter over the wrecks, eh? Rough water for her.
Ships are going onto the North Headland in fog. A skipper at North Cove says somebody lights a lamp there.
If you carry the Couriers' tube, hand it on at the square. Fresh legs beat proud ones, and bandits watch the long roads.
The Couriers beat the wagons. Sound to Waste in a day, paw to paw. The Carters' Yard keeper bought the round, fair play to him.
The runners came over the Waste like water down a wadi. Peace on their pads, every one.
Wagons won the post, cousin. Dead rock luck for the runners. Next season, they say.
Go to the weir at dusk with friends and a strong back, no? The guards run when they're outnumbered, and the stakes come out easy in the mud.
The eels are up Withy Creek again, thick as reeds. Mud and eels, it's a fair-dry spring after all.
Eels are dear at the Fish Hall. Somebody pulled their weir out of the fens.
Fenshore has a share of the Fish Hall's eels now. Fair price, if you ask me.
No eels this spring. The skipper at Fen Shore landing thinks somebody's stopped them on the river.
They say a Quickened wolf walks through the Heights' walls and takes pledges. Lock your strongroom, for all the good it does.
There's an old street under the Heights, from before the walls. The Sunken Street. Folk say it runs further than anybody's walked.
Vance House let the Sump pledges go. A wolf put it to the lender plain, they say, and the lender listened.
Ridgemere caught its wall-walking thief. A pup, they say, no Gift at all. Short-weighed magic, that.
The Heights swear it was a Quickened thief. Somebody's writing to the Wardens. Bright One keep us all.
Pledges vanishing from a locked room on the Rise. The lender at Vance House wants a plain answer.
If you go after the char thieves, go at night and go below the tarn. They dry what they steal by a fire, cousin, and a fire shows.
Upper hearths charcoal at half price in the city. Dead rock luck, or somebody's hand in it. Deep, I'd say the hand.
The charcoal store pays the hill colliers by the sack now. Dearer coal, and no strangers at the yard door.
Frosthollow charcoal on the Frosthollow square, Marketday. Deep and plain, the way it should be, stone.
Greenholt wagons carry the Upper hearths' charcoal too now. Fair price, if not full weight for the hill folk.
The Upper hearths' charcoal sells at half in the city. The colliers want somebody to find out why.
